Alumni talk Abolish Greek Life movement, possibility of reform 6 years later

Daily file photo by Allie Goulding
In summer 2020, an Instagram account named @abolishnugreeklife began posting anonymous accounts of students’ negative experiences in fraternities and sororities. Many described facing racism and sexual misconduct.
Ella Smith, Reporter
November 24, 2026

Content warning: This article contains discussions of sexual assault.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:28
Instaread

After Skylar Waldron (Weinberg ’24) transferred to Northwestern in 2020, she found herself as just one of two remaining members of Kappa Kappa Gamma, becoming the chapter’s vice president by default and later serving as president.

The mass exodus was propelled by a University-wide reckoning over Greek life. Now, six years later, fraternities and sororities are drawing renewed scrutiny nationwide after an alleged sexual assault at Cornell University. 

Former NU students who witnessed the Abolish Greek Life movement firsthand are now grappling with its legacy. Looking back on her experience, Waldron said she does not regret her decision to stay affiliated with her sorority.

“I chose to stay because there is no other place where women have a safe space with each other that is only women or only non-binary people,” Waldron said. “This is the only place we have where we can exclude cis(gender)-men.”

In summer  2020, an Instagram account named @abolishnugreeklife began posting anonymous accounts of students’ negative experiences in fraternities and sororities. Many described facing racism and sexual misconduct.

The ensuing controversy led to member disaffiliations and the disbandment of entire chapters. 

The University converted six Greek life houses into residence halls ahead of the 2021-22 school year. Later, students demonstrated on campus, calling for the abolition of Greek life at NU. The protests followed fall 2021 reports of non-consensual druggings at the houses of Alpha Epsilon Pi and Sigma Alpha Epsilon.

Waldron’s sorority suspended operations, with members voting to surrender the chapter’s charter in February 2022.

For Nick Papandreou (Medill ’22), former president of Sigma Phi Epsilon and 2021 president of the Interfraternity Council, the movement encouraged fraternity leaders to ensure their spaces positively influenced campus life. 

“Bad things do happen in fraternity spaces,” Papandreou said. “But my thought was firmly of the belief that we can solve for that. This is a problem. We’ve got two sides. We can find a good middle ground approach.”

Papendreou said he and other fraternity leaders were “very successful at the time” in addressing the Abolish Greek Life movement’s concerns. He said he pushed for greater transparency, appropriate sanctions, targeted education and increased dialogue between fraternities and other student organizations.

He added that although continued reported misconduct within fraternities demonstrates the need for oversight, these instances and resulting punishments prove “the system is working” to address concerns surrounding fraternities. 

“The approach I had was we need more focus on (fraternities), more controls placed on them to make sure that we are leveraging and benefiting from all the good things that those organizations do provide,” Papendreou said. 

Former Daily staffer Ada Ogbonna (Medill ’23) served as vice president of Associated Student Government and helped spearhead the Abolish Greek Life movement. She said she personally knew those who started the anonymous Instagram account. 

She said increased safety protocols within Greek life were insufficient, making abolition the only option.

“At the end of the day, you can’t dialogue your way out of people spiking drinks,” Ogbonna said. “You can only have so many conversations around ‘You shouldn’t sexually assault people when they’re inebriated.’”

Looking back, she said she believes the University did not and has not done enough to protect vulnerable students.

Waldron said fraternities were — and remain — significantly more problematic than sororities.

“I am 100% in alignment with disbanding all the frats. I think they’re disgusting,” Waldron said. “I think they should absolutely be banned. There’s no reason for them.”

Waldron said she felt the Abolish Greek Life movement unfairly punished sororities for fraternities’ mistakes. She added that she believes the movement’s only success was “(finding) a way to destroy a way that women could be together.”

She expressed concern over Greek life abolition unless the movement’s leaders discover how to replicate the security and acceptance of women-only spaces.

For Papandreou, the problems within fraternities do not justify abolishing them altogether, he said.

“I cannot support abolition because in any given group of people, take fraternities or beyond, there’s always going to be good guys, there’s always going to be bad guys, and the vast majority of people are in the middle. And they’re not bad guys,” he said. “I think it’s unfair to those — call it 80%, 90%, whatever percent of people who are not bad guys — to abolish the fraternity.”

Waldron said she doesn’t think “men keep each other accountable in the way that women do,” making fraternity culture unfixable.

“I don’t think you can reform something that is known for assault,” she said. 

Hope O’Conner (Weinberg ’22), a former president of the Zeta Tau Alpha chapter at NU who pushed for its disbandment at the time, said issues within Greek life “are always going to persist.”

She added that the younger generation of undergraduate students might not share the same perspective as those who witnessed the movement during her time at NU. 

“I think that there’s a level of knowledge and understanding that younger, newer Northwestern community members won’t have until something horrible comes around again,” she said. 

Interfraternity Council President Brayden Golder said the Abolish Greek Life movement has had a lasting impact on campus. 

“Maybe we needed to get rid of those bad apples and kind of restart our culture because there’s a lot of good in these communities,” Golder said. 

Since the Cornell case garnered national attention, Golder said he has urged the University community to give members of Greek chapters “a little grace.” 

He added that he hopes the NU student body recognizes the differences between Greek life at NU and other universities. 

“There (were) people that wanted to protest at our fraternities,” Golder said. 

He said students shouldn’t take what happened at Cornell and apply it to all fraternities, including those on campus. 

Ogbonna emphasized she wants to see the movement for abolition continue. 

While she said she acknowledges the challenges of overturning an institution that provides funding and recognition to the University, she said she trusts the next generation of students to advance the movement she helped build.

“I have full confidence in the students of Northwestern today to advocate for themselves and fight for what’s best for them on campus,” she said. “If Greek life is making campus unsafe, do something about it. The same way that we did when it was making our campus unsafe.”

Jenny Marquez contributed reporting.

Email: ellasmith2030@u.northwestern.edu
